items.name: Al Bunt
items.res: Book the room, not the room type.
items.line: Al Bunt (البنط), a concept boutique hotel in a Hijazi coral-stone house in Jeddah Al-Balad, named after Bab Al-Bunt, the sea gate where every traveller arrived. The real problem: Middle East hotels take about half their bookings through OTAs and pay up to 28% for each, while Saudi rates fell 12% as licensed hotels hit a record. On an OTA a house of 7 one-of-a-kind rooms becomes “Deluxe Double, SAR 389”. So every room has a name and a window, and you can only choose it by name direct, on WhatsApp with the host.

items.name: Daffa
items.res: Safety you can see before you sail
items.line: Daffa (دفّة, the helm), a concept brand for private family boat trips in Hurghada, for Gulf families first. The real problem: sea trips there are sold by brokers, not brands, and the fear is recent: a yacht capsized in November 2024 and a tourist submarine sank off Hurghada in March 2025, while Saudi visitors to Egypt passed 1.2 million in 2025. So the boat is your family’s only, and the safety is in front of your eyes before you sail: a jacket fitted for each child on the dock, the captain’s name and licence on WhatsApp the night before, live location all trip.

items.name: Shaqa Omry
items.res: Everyone sees who paid. So everyone pays.
items.line: Shaqa Omry (شقا عمري, “my life’s savings”), a concept app for the jameya (جمعية), the rotating savings circle: 43% of Egyptians with savings are in one, even though 77.6% of adults now have an account. It still runs on one organiser, a notebook and WhatsApp: she chases every late payer, it’s embarrassing, and when it breaks it breaks friendships or ends in court. The apps that exist match you with strangers; this one is for the jameya you already have with your own people. Every payment shows as paid or late to the whole group, so nobody has to chase: the quiet embarrassment does it, and people pay on time or early.

items.name: Sahalat
items.res: Every post answers one question.
items.line: A content pitch for Sahalat (سهالات), a Saudi platform that compares home and personal finance offers. Their feed used one template on every post; the proposal gives each post one question a home buyer really has: same instalment, not the same cost · want to buy a house? · what the bank reads in your file · remember the name. 3D coins and a key built on their mark, an AI photo, Saudi dialect and a new Arabic typeface (Alexandria). The pitch did not close.

items.name: Wba3dein?
items.res: Arabic they want to read.
items.line: Wba3dein? (⁨وبعدين؟⁩, “and then what?”), a concept reading app for Gulf kids aged 6 to 10 in English-medium schools. English wins their day: 68% of young Gulf Arabs use it more than Arabic, only 3 of 17 Outstanding Dubai schools were Good in Arabic, and the apps that exist teach letters, not wanting. At 9, the share of kids who love reading drops from 40% to 28%, and 89% love the books they chose. So the story stops at a fork, the choice opens only when he reads it aloud, and ten stories with his choices print as a real book with his name on the cover. The parent’s line «⁨روح اقرا!⁩» becomes the kid’s own «⁨وبعدين؟⁩».
